payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Who Wrote the English Sentences

¶1 Last Tuesday the Ambervale Prize announced its shortlist, and the press release named six novels, six authors, and six publishers, but not one translator. Four of those six books were written in languages the jury does not read. I know this because I translated one of them. My name appears on page four of the paperback, in a typeface smaller than the one used to describe the paper stock.

¶2 Readers sometimes imagine translation as a kind of plumbing: the words flow in one end of the pipe in Norwegian and come out the other end in English, and the translator merely checks for leaks. The image is comforting, and it is wrong. A sentence in one language is not a container with a fixed amount of meaning inside it; it is a set of choices that a second language cannot reproduce but can only answer. When the Norwegian novelist Sigrun Aalvik wrote that her heroine "went out into the weather," she used a verb that in her dialect also means to quarrel. English has no such verb. I had to decide whether the woman walked into a storm or into an argument, and whichever I chose, the English reader would believe the author had chosen it.

¶3 Consider the scale of the problem. Aalvik's novel runs to roughly ninety thousand words, and I made, by my own rough count, something near forty decisions a page that no dictionary could make for me: where to break a sentence, which of three possible synonyms carried the right chill, whether a joke survived or had to be replaced with a different joke. Multiply that by three hundred pages and you arrive at an English book that shares a plot and a spirit with the Norwegian one but shares none of its sentences. Every sentence the English reader admires, I wrote. Every sentence the reader finds clumsy, I also wrote.

¶4 I can hear the objection, because I have made it myself at dinner parties: the story, the characters, the architecture of the book belong to Aalvik, and the translator is at most a skilled carpenter working from her drawings. There is something to this. I did not invent the heroine, and I would not want credit for her. But a carpenter who selects every board, every joint, and every finish, and whose work the client lives inside for years, is not usually left off the plaque. Architecture is credited; so is the building.

¶5 Why, then, does the convention of the invisible translator persist? Partly because publishers fear that a second name on the cover warns the buyer that the book is foreign, and foreign, in the sales meeting, means difficult. Partly because reviewers, who seldom read the original, find it easier to praise "the author's luminous prose" than to admit they are praising prose whose author they cannot identify. And partly, I confess, because translators themselves have cultivated a monkish modesty, as though visibility were a kind of vanity. The effect is circular: because we are unnamed, we seem unimportant, and because we seem unimportant, nobody thinks to name us.

¶6 I am not asking for the author's name to be removed, or shrunk, or shared with mine in some awkward hyphenated compound. I am asking for a line of type on the front of the book, the same size as the blurb from a novelist nobody has heard of, that says who wrote the English sentences. If you run a prize, name the translator in the press release. If you review books, say which words you are actually quoting. And if you are a reader who has ever loved a novel written in a language you do not speak, you have already loved a translator's work; you simply were not told whom to thank.

provenance.venue_alias: The Margin (a personal blog on translation)
provenance.note: Entirely fictional writer, prize, novelist and figures.

blueprint.speaker: Ines Halvorsen, a literary translator from Norwegian into English who writes a long-form blog called The Margin
blueprint.audience: readers of literary fiction, book reviewers, prize administrators and publishers, plus fellow translators
blueprint.exigence: The fictional Ambervale Prize announced its shortlist in a press release that named authors and publishers but no translators, though the writer translated one of the shortlisted novels
blueprint.purpose: To persuade readers and the publishing world that translators are co-authors of the English text and should be named on covers, in press releases and in reviews
blueprint.context: A personal blog post written in the week after the shortlist announcement, drawing on the writer's own experience translating a novel by the fictional Norwegian novelist Sigrun Aalvik
blueprint.claim: Because every English sentence in a translated novel is the translator's decision, translators are authors of the books readers actually read, and their invisibility is a chosen convention that should be reversed by naming them
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Opens with the prize anecdote showing the omission (P1); dismantles the plumbing model of translation and shows through the 'weather' example that translation is a chain of authorial choices (P2); scales that example up with a count of decisions to argue the English sentences are the translator's (P3); concedes the author owns story and characters but rebuts through the carpenter analogy (P4); asks why invisibility persists and enumerates three causes that form a circle (P5); shifts to a modest proposal and direct address to prize runners, reviewers and readers (P6)
evidence_types: specific textual example from a translation
rough self-reported count presented as a statistic

devices.function: Establishes the exigence and the writer's firsthand stake through the prize press release
The translator's name is smaller than the note about paper stock, exposing the absurd priority of credit
The plumbing analogy states the popular view so it can be rejected
Short sentences after long ones deliver the verdict bluntly
Redefines a sentence as a set of choices rather than a container of meaning
The 'went out into the weather' example shows one authorial choice forced on the translator
The rough count of forty decisions a page scales the single example into a book-wide claim
Matching fronted clauses claim authorship of both praise and blame
Admired versus clumsy sentences both end in 'I wrote'
Grants the author's ownership of story and characters, then rebuts with the carpenter analogy
'There is something to this' concedes minimally before the turn
Carpenter and architect analogy reframes the translator's contribution as creditable craft
Pivots from establishing authorship to diagnosing why it goes uncredited
Three 'partly' causes organize the diagnosis
Shows the three causes forming a self-reinforcing circle
The colon announces the circular explanation that the two following clauses enact
Limits the proposal to avoid seeming to displace the author
Assigns concrete actions to prize runners, reviewers and readers
Repeated 'If you...' clauses make the call to action feel orderly and modest
Reminds readers they have already loved a translator's work without knowing it

ALTON original passage
Who Else Will Come: On Conrad Weil's Siren on the Ridge

¶1 The pager goes off at ten past two in the morning, and for eleven years my first thought was never about the fire but about who else would come. In Brannock County, where I served with the Marrow Creek Volunteer Fire Company until my knees retired me, a structure fire draws whoever is awake, sober, and within fifteen miles. Some nights that is nine people; some nights it is three. Conrad Weil's new book, Siren on the Ridge, is the first account I have read that understands this arithmetic, and it deserves a wide readership among the county commissioners who will decide, over the next decade, whether rural counties keep a volunteer fire service at all.

¶2 Weil's reporting is the book's great strength. He spent two years riding with departments in six counties across three states, and he lets the volunteers speak in their own flat, unsentimental voices. The numbers he gathers are grim: at one station the average age of a responder rose from thirty-four to fifty-seven in twenty years, and the roster shrank from twenty-two names to nine. He describes a chief who answers calls alone because there is no one else, and a township that dissolved its company and now waits forty minutes for an engine from the next county. These are not isolated anecdotes; they are the shape of the thing.

¶3 Where the book falters is in its diagnosis. Weil concludes that the volunteer model is simply obsolete, a relic of a time when men worked within walking distance of the station and could leave the mill when the whistle blew, and he argues that counties should accept the inevitable and hire paid crews. I grant that the old pattern is gone; nobody leaves a shift at a distribution warehouse forty miles away to answer a brush fire. But obsolete is the wrong word for a system that has been quietly loaded with burdens it was never designed to carry. The state now requires one hundred eighty hours of certified training before a recruit may enter a burning building, up from forty when I joined. The company must also buy its own equipment, which means that the same nine people who fight the fires also run the fish fry, the raffle, the mailer, and the pancake breakfast that pays for the air packs. We did not lose volunteers because people stopped caring about their neighbors. We lost them because we asked each one to be a firefighter, a fundraiser, a mechanic, and a grant writer, and then wondered why only retirees had the hours.

¶4 Asking a fire company to sell raffle tickets for its own breathing apparatus is like asking a lifeguard to run a lemonade stand to pay for the pool. The absurdity would be obvious anywhere else. Yet Weil treats the fundraising burden as a charming folkway rather than the structural failure it is, and so he never asks the question that matters: what happens to the roster when the county, not the fish fry, buys the truck?

¶5 We have some evidence, and it is more hopeful than Weil allows. Tillery County, two hours north of us, passed a modest fire levy six years ago, roughly the price of a tank of gas per household per year, and used it to cover equipment and to reimburse recruits for their training hours. Its volunteer roster has grown by a third since, and the average age of a new recruit is twenty-nine. The people were there all along. They had simply been priced out of serving.

¶6 So read Siren on the Ridge for its portraits, which are honest and often moving, and for its warning, which is overdue. But read it skeptically when it reaches for the obituary. Volunteer fire service is not dying of old age; it is being starved, and starvation, unlike age, has a remedy. If you sit on a county board, the remedy is in your budget. The pager will go off tonight somewhere in your district, and the only question that matters is who else will come.

provenance.note: Original review essay of a fictional book, Siren on the Ridge by fictional author Conrad Weil. All names, places and figures are invented.

blueprint.speaker: Delia Hartsook, a columnist for a fictional regional quarterly and a former volunteer firefighter with the Marrow Creek Volunteer Fire Company in fictional Brannock County
blueprint.audience: Readers of a rural regional magazine, especially county commissioners and board members who control fire-service budgets
blueprint.exigence: The publication of a new book, Siren on the Ridge by fictional author Conrad Weil, which argues that the volunteer fire model is obsolete and should be replaced with paid crews
blueprint.purpose: To praise the book's reporting while rejecting its diagnosis, and to persuade county officials that volunteer departments are being starved by unfunded burdens that modest public funding can relieve
blueprint.context: Rural counties facing shrinking, aging volunteer rosters, rising state training requirements, and equipment costs covered by fundraising
blueprint.claim: Volunteer fire service is not obsolete; it is failing because it has been loaded with fundraising and training burdens it was never designed to carry, and those burdens can be lifted by county funding
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Opens with firsthand anecdote establishing credibility and stakes (P1); credits the book's reporting and grim numbers (P2); concedes the old pattern is gone but rebuts the diagnosis of obsolescence by identifying training and fundraising burdens (P3); uses an analogy to expose the absurdity of self-funded equipment and poses the question the book never asks (P4); answers that question with the Tillery County counterexample (P5); delivers the verdict on the book and a direct appeal to county boards (P6)

Weil's grim numbers establish the problem; Tillery's numbers support the writer's remedy
Colons introduce the grim figures and the unasked question with emphasis
Grants that the old pattern is gone, then rejects 'obsolete' as the wrong diagnosis
Lists of fundraising events and roles pile up to show the burden on volunteers
'We did not lose... We lost...' contrasts apathy with overburden
Parallel openings sharpen the corrected diagnosis
Lifeguard and lemonade stand expose the absurdity of self-funded equipment
Poses the question the book fails to ask, setting up paragraph 5
Moves from critical to hopeful as evidence of a remedy is introduced
Two short sentences after longer ones deliver the point with force
'Reaches for the obituary' and 'being starved' contrast premature death-notice with preventable neglect
Speaks directly to county board members to urge action
'Who else would come' frames the essay and closes it

payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Standing on Her Work

¶1 One Tuesday last October, a date-formatting library called tidyclock vanished from the public package registry, and by morning several thousand websites could no longer tell their users what day it was. Its sole maintainer, a retired schoolteacher in Pell Harbor, had deleted it after a decade of unpaid work and one rude bug report too many. Desmond Alcock's new book, Nobody's Job, opens with that night, and it is the right place to begin. I spent nine years maintaining a small text-parsing library used by companies I was never allowed to name, so I read Alcock with the uneasy attention of a patient reading her own chart.

¶2 The book's first half is a diagnosis, and it is a good one. Alcock surveyed four hundred of the most heavily downloaded packages in three programming languages and found that more than half depended on a single active volunteer. He calls these projects load-bearing walls that no inspector has visited, and the metaphor earns its keep: the walls are hidden inside the plaster of every bank, hospital, and school district that runs code on top of them. Nobody chose this arrangement. It accreted, one convenient download at a time, until the whole structure rested on the patience of people who could stop at any moment and owed us nothing if they did.

¶3 It is in the second half, where Alcock turns from diagnosis to cure, that the book loses its footing. His remedy is sponsorship: corporations that profit from open-source software should fund its maintainers, and he describes several foundations that already do so. I will grant that money has saved projects. A stipend kept at least one widely used encryption library alive after its maintainer nearly quit, and Alcock tells that story well. But a stipend changes what the work is. Consider the neighbor who shovels the shared walkway every winter because no one else will; the day you start paying her, the shoveling becomes a service, the snow becomes her problem, and you acquire the right to complain about ice. Sponsorship converts a gift into a contract, and the contract arrives written in the sponsor's priorities, not the project's.

¶4 I know something about how such gifts are received. In nine years I received roughly four thousand bug reports, most of them phrased as demands, several of them threatening, and one, from a hospital network in a city I have never visited, that began with the words "thank you." One. Did any of those four thousand correspondents imagine that a person, rather than a department, was reading them at eleven at night? Alcock understands this loneliness better than any writer I have read, which is precisely why his faith in a check is so puzzling.

¶5 The better cure is already visible in the margins of his own book, though he never names it. The institutions that depend on these libraries do not lack money; they lack a sense that the maintenance is theirs to do. A regional bank runs tidyclock on its login page, employs ninety engineers, and has never assigned one of them a Friday afternoon to review tidyclock's open issues. Volunteer fire departments survive not because the town mails a check to the one person who owns a hose but because the people whose houses would burn show up for the drills. The obligation should attach to dependence, not to profit, and it should be paid in hours, not dollars. This will not rescue every project, and the smallest libraries will still rely on the stubbornness of individuals; but it would spread the weight across the walls that bear it.

¶6 Nobody's Job deserves the wide readership it will probably get. Read it for the first half, which will frighten you in the right way, and argue with the second, which will comfort you in the wrong one. The retired schoolteacher in Pell Harbor did not need a sponsor. She needed the several thousand of us who were standing on her work to notice that we were.

blueprint.speaker: Imogen Tarrow, a former volunteer maintainer of a small text-parsing library for nine years, now writing criticism for a general-interest quarterly
blueprint.audience: Educated general readers of a literary and ideas quarterly, most of whom use software built on volunteer-maintained libraries without knowing it, including managers and engineers at the institutions that depend on such code
blueprint.exigence: The publication of Desmond Alcock's book Nobody's Job, which opens with the recent collapse of thousands of websites after the lone maintainer of the tidyclock library deleted it
blueprint.purpose: To recommend the book's diagnosis of fragile volunteer infrastructure while rejecting its prescribed cure of corporate sponsorship, and to propose instead that dependent institutions contribute maintenance labor
blueprint.context: A review essay in The Harrowgate Quarterly, written shortly after a widely noticed outage caused by a single volunteer quitting
blueprint.claim: Alcock is right that critical software rests on unseen, unpaid individuals, but wrong that money is the remedy; the obligation to maintain should attach to dependence and be paid in hours by the institutions that rely on the code.
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Paragraph 1 opens with the tidyclock anecdote and establishes the reviewer's ethos as a former maintainer. Paragraph 2 endorses the book's diagnosis (survey, load-bearing-walls metaphor). Paragraph 3 pivots to the book's prescription, concedes that money has helped, then rebuts with the shoveling analogy: payment converts a gift into a contract. Paragraph 4 shifts to personal testimony about ungrateful bug reports to show that the real deficit is recognition, not cash, and links that back to the critique. Paragraph 5 supplies the alternative cure (institutions lending hours, volunteer fire department analogy) with a qualification of its limits. Paragraph 6 renders the verdict and returns to the schoolteacher of the opening.

payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
A Fence Around an Hour

¶1 The pledge card came in the same envelope as the library's autumn newsletter, printed on oatmeal-colored stock with a line for each member of the household to sign. "Screens Down at Supper," it read, and underneath, in smaller type, "Give your children back the table." I read it twice at my own kitchen table, phone face down beside the sugar bowl, and felt the particular unease of someone who agrees with a proposal and distrusts its wording. Give the children back the table? Who, exactly, had taken it from them?

¶2 My grandmother, Solveig Arnesen, bought her first radio in the autumn of 1938, a walnut cabinet set that cost her, according to the household ledger she kept in a looping hand, thirty-one dollars and forty cents. The ledger records the purchase on a Tuesday. By the following Sunday a second entry appears, not a sum but a sentence: "No set from six to seven. All of us." The family story is that my grandfather, not the children, had been the trouble, sitting with his ear to the speaker through an entire meal while the program crackled about grain prices and a prizefight in a city none of them would ever see. The rule she wrote was not a punishment for the young. It was a fence she built around an hour, and she built it to keep herself and her husband inside as much as anyone.

¶3 The pattern repeated itself with a regularity that would be comic if it were not so instructive. In 1954 the telephone arrived, and my mother remembers the cord unplugged at a quarter to six and coiled on top of the icebox like a sleeping cat. In 1967 the television came, and with it a new entry in a new ledger, this time in my mother's hand: "Set off at supper, no exceptions, Dad included." Each machine was a stranger at the door, and each time the household did the same thing: it did not bar the stranger, it told the stranger when to call. The radio stayed; the telephone stayed; the television, heaven help us, stayed. What changed was that a single hour was marked off as belonging to the people at the table rather than to the voices coming through the wall.

¶4 There is a difference, I think, between a curfew and a ritual, and the difference matters more than the hour chosen. A curfew is a rule imposed on someone by someone else; it names a suspect and a warden. A ritual is a thing a group does together, on purpose, at a set time, because doing it together is the point. The mill at the foot of Carrow Bend used to blow its whistle at noon, and nobody heard that whistle as an accusation; it was simply the sound of everyone stopping at once. My grandmother's "All of us" was a whistle, not a warrant.

¶5 I will concede that the ledgers do not record a single happy supper. They record cabbage and coal and the price of shoes, and the surviving letters mention more than one meal eaten in a silence that was sullen rather than peaceful, teenagers and tired parents with nothing to say and a forbidden radio in the next room. Nostalgia would have me believe that the quiet hour produced conversation; the evidence suggests only that it produced attendance. But attendance, it turns out, is not nothing. The sullen suppers of 1941 are the ones my mother still describes in detail, down to the pattern on the oilcloth, and she cannot describe a single evening when the set was on.

¶6 So I will sign the card, and I would urge you to sign it as well, though I would ask you to take a pen and cross out the second line before you do. Do not give the children back the table. Sit down at it yourself, phone in the drawer, and let them see you, every night, until the hour belongs to all of you and nobody remembers whom it was meant to protect. My grandmother knew this in 1938 with a radio she could barely afford. The machine has changed. The fence has not.

blueprint.speaker: Imogen Halvorsen, a retired schoolteacher and amateur family historian in the fictional mill town of Carrow Bend, who has kept her grandmother's household ledgers and letters
blueprint.audience: Readers of a community magazine, mostly parents and grandparents, who have just received the public library's 'Screens Down at Supper' pledge card
blueprint.exigence: The Carrow Bend Public Library's pledge drive asks households to put screens away at supper 'to give your children back the table'; the writer agrees with the practice but objects to the wording, which casts children as the problem
blueprint.purpose: To persuade readers to sign the pledge but to reframe it as a shared household ritual that binds adults as much as children, using three generations of family history as evidence
blueprint.context: A historical-narrative essay published in a small-town quarterly magazine; the writer narrates her family's responses to the arrival of the radio (1938), the telephone (1954) and the television (1967) and draws a lesson for the present
blueprint.claim: Every generation has had to fence off the supper hour from a new machine, and the fences that held were rituals kept by the whole household, not curfews imposed on the young; the difference between a curfew and a ritual matters more than the hour chosen
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: P1 presents the occasion (the pledge card) and the writer's unease with its wording, posed as questions. P2 narrates the 1938 radio anecdote, revealing that the grandfather, not the children, was the problem and that the rule applied to everyone. payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Testimony on Ordinance 14-B

[1] Good evening, members of the Larkhaven City Council. [2] My name is Odile Strand, and I have lived on Quarry Hill Road for twenty-two years. [3] Tonight I want to talk about lights.

[4] Every second Saturday, the Larkhaven Stargazers Club sets up telescopes in the gravel lot behind the public library. [5] Ten years ago, we could show visitors the faint smudge of the Andromeda galaxy without much trouble. [6] Since the city installed the new white LED globes along Cutler Avenue, that smudge has disappeared from our lot entirely. [7] Last spring a nine-year-old girl looked through my eyepiece, saw only a gray haze, and asked whether the telescope was broken.

[8] The problem is not that the lights are on but where they point. [9] The Cutler Avenue fixtures are uncovered globes that throw about a third of their light sideways and upward, where it lights nothing but the sky. [10] The town of Fenwick Ridge, forty miles north, replaced its globes with fully shielded fixtures and reported that its electricity bill for street lighting dropped by 18 percent. [11] Shielded fixtures, which aim light downward toward the street, they cost about the same as the globes the city currently uses and they also last just as long as the globes do.

[12] Anyway, that is basically all I have got, so thanks for listening to me ramble.

ALTON original passage
What the Shoreline Taught Us: A Report on Merrow Point's Retreating Coast

[1] The ocean has always been a powerful force in human history. [2] This fall, our environmental science class spent nine weeks measuring the bluffs along Gannet Road. [3] We used survey stakes, old aerial photographs from the town library, and interviews with eleven residents. [4] What we found out and discovered in the end was that the bluff edge has moved back an average of about two feet every single year since 1990.

[5] The town's first answer to erosion was the concrete seawall built below Pell Street in 1998. [6] The wall protected the houses directly behind it for many years. [7] Anyone who still thinks walls are the answer simply has not looked at the beach. [8] Waves bouncing off the concrete have scoured away the sand in front of it, and the beach at Pell Street has nearly vanished.

[9] Dune restoration is a better way to protect the coast. [10] Last spring, volunteers planted beach grass and set sand fences along the north end of Little Cove. [11] Our stake measurements there showed that the bluff lost less than four inches this year, compared with two feet near the seawall. [12] The town has also moved the Gannet Road pump station 200 feet inland, and the lifeguard tower now sits on movable skids.

[13] Moving buildings is expensive. [14] Rebuilding them after a storm costs more. [15] Our class recommends that the council fund more dune planting and begin planning which structures should move first.

The Gearhounds: A First-Season Report

[1] Last August, eleven students and one chemistry teacher met in the back corner of the woodshop at Harlow Creek High School with a donated toolbox, two secondhand motor kits, and no idea how to build a robot. [2] Eight months later, our robot, which we named Marmalade because of its orange zip ties, placed ninth out of twenty-six teams at the Tri-County Build Challenge in Dunmore. [3] This report is about what the Gearhounds did this year and some things that happened. [4] I am writing it because the Student Activities Board asked every new club for a summary before it votes on next year's budgets.

[5] The team spent September and October learning basics: how to wire a motor controller, how to read a gear ratio, how to keep a chassis from twisting. [6] Our first drive base, finished in November, could not turn left. [7] Instead of starting over, we traced the problem to a mismatched pair of wheels and swapped them in a single afternoon. [8] By February, Marmalade could lift a foam block, drive over a ramp, and park itself inside a taped square, the three tasks the competition required. [9] Honestly, the judges were kind of blown away that a first-year team even showed up with a working bot.

[10] The members learned a great deal from the season. [11] Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before, by March they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day. [12] Our faculty adviser, Ms. Delacroix-Tam, kept a sign-in sheet, and attendance never dropped below nine members, even during exam week.

[13] Next year the team needs a locking storage cabinet, a second set of batteries, and roughly 900 dollars for competition registration. [14] The board should fund us because robotics is obviously the coolest club at the school and everyone knows it. [15] We are not asking for a new room or a new teacher; we are asking for a shelf, a charger, and a chance to finish what we started.
